name: Sutherlandia (Sutherlandia frutescens, cancer bush)
short: HIV trial: more infection days than placebo, from 2 tuberculosis cases on isoniazid prevention. In 12 healthy men it lowered levels of the HIV drug atazanavir; lab and rat data suggest others.
text: In a 24-week double-blind, placebo-controlled safety trial in South African adults with HIV and CD4 counts above 350 (107 analysed), dried Sutherlandia taken by mouth did not change HIV viral load, but the burden of infection (days of infection-related events) was greater than with placebo (p = 0.045), attributed to two cases of tuberculosis in people taking isoniazid preventive therapy; the authors said a possible interaction with isoniazid preventive therapy needs further evaluation and identified no other safety issues. The abstract does not say whether participants were taking antiretroviral medicines. In a study in 12 healthy men, 12 days of milled Sutherlandia (taken twice daily from day 3 to day 14) lowered exposure to a single dose of the HIV protease inhibitor atazanavir (geometric mean ratios 0.783 for peak level and 0.801 for total exposure, with confidence intervals reaching 1.00 and 1.01; the authors said both intervals fell below the limits of their 0.8 to 1.25 no-effect boundary, indicating a significant reduction), which the authors said may potentially result in subtherapeutic levels and reduced anti-HIV efficacy. In a 3-month placebo-controlled pilot trial in 25 healthy adults, general adverse events did not differ significantly between Sutherlandia leaf powder capsules and placebo. Laboratory and animal studies add further possible interactions that have not been tested in patients: extracts inhibited several drug-metabolising liver enzymes (including CYP3A4/5) and drug transporters in human liver preparations and cell lines, and in rats 5 days of Sutherlandia halved blood levels of the HIV medicine nevirapine.
